lead: Parseval's theorem is an energy accounting rule. The energy or average power of a signal can be computed either from its time waveform or from its Fourier spectrum, and the two answers match. Engineers use it to find signal energy without integrating in time, to read how energy is spread over frequency, and to define bandwidth for filters and communication links. This chapter states the rule for continuous-time Fourier transforms and Fourier series, then defines the energy spectral density and power spectral density.
prereq: You need: energy and power signals from Unit 1; Fourier series from 3.1; Fourier transform from 3.2; and transform properties from 3.3.

blocks.text: For a continuous-time signal x(t), define the total energy E and the average power P by the limits below. The signal may be real or complex; |x(t)|² is the squared magnitude.

blocks.where: x(t) is the signal; E is energy in joules (J) if x is in volts across 1 Ω; P is average power in watts (W); T is the averaging window length in seconds (s).

blocks.text: An energy signal has 0 < E < ∞. Its average power is zero. A power signal has 0 < P < ∞. Its total energy is infinite. A pulse e^{−3t}u(t) is an energy signal, where u(t) is the unit step. A sine wave and a step are power signals.

These names decide which Parseval form applies. Use the energy form for pulses and finite-duration signals. Use the power form for periodic signals and signals that run forever with finite average power.

Take the Fourier transform pair X(ω)=∫x(t)e^{−jωt}dt and x(t)=(1/2π)∫X(ω)e^{jωt}dω. Here ω is angular frequency in rad/s. Parseval's theorem for an energy signal says the energy computed in time equals the scaled area under |X(ω)|² on the frequency axis.

blocks.where: E is total energy in J; X(ω) is the Fourier transform of x(t); |X(ω)|² is the energy spectral density; the factor 1/2π comes from the inverse transform convention above.

blocks.text: For a periodic signal with period T0 and exponential Fourier series x(t)=Σ cₙ e^{j n ω0 t}, average power is the sum of squared coefficient magnitudes. Here ω0=2π/T0 is the fundamental angular frequency in rad/s, and cₙ is the n-th Fourier coefficient.

blocks.where: P is average power in W; T0 is the period in s; cₙ=(1/T0)∫<sub>T0</sub>x(t)e^{−j n ω0 t}dt; the sum is over all integers n.

blocks.text: The energy spectral density (ESD) of an energy signal is |X(ω)|². It tells how much energy lies in a small band dω around ω. Its area, after the 1/2π scale, is total energy.

blocks.where: ESD(ω) has units J per (rad/s) for a 1 Ω reference; ω is in rad/s.

blocks.text: For a power signal, use a truncated version x_T(t) that is zero outside |t|≤T/2. Its Fourier transform is X_T(ω). The PSD is the limit below. Average power is the 1/2π-scaled area under PSD.

blocks.where: PSD(ω) has units W per (rad/s); T is the truncation length in s; X_T(ω) is the transform of x_T(t).

blocks.text: For a periodic signal the spectrum is a line spectrum at nω0, and each line carries power |cₙ|². Bandwidth from cumulative energy: choose B so the band |ω|≤B holds a fraction η of total energy, with 0<η<1. Then ∫<sub>−B</sub><sup>B</sup>ESD(ω)dω = η(2πE). The smallest such B is the η-energy bandwidth. The same idea with PSD gives power bandwidth.

figure.caption: The curve is |X(ω)|²=1/(9+ω²) for x(t)=e^{−3t}u(t). The scaled two-sided area (1/2π)∫|X(ω)|²dω is the energy 1/6 J.

spec.aria: For x(t)=e^{-3t}u(t), the energy spectral density 1/(9+ω²) peaks at ω=0 and its scaled area equals the energy 1/6 J.

examples.question: For x(t)=e^{−3t}u(t), compute the total energy E from the time waveform. Then verify Parseval's theorem using X(ω)=1/(3+jω).
steps: For t≥0, |x(t)|²=e^{−6t}; for t<0 it is zero. Thus E=∫<sub>0</sub><sup>∞</sup> e^{−6t}dt.
Parseval side: (1/2π)∫<sub>−∞</sub><sup>∞</sup> 1/(9+ω²)dω. Use ∫du/(a²+u²)=(1/a)tan^{−1}(u/a). Here a=3, so the integral over all ω is π/3.
examples.answer: E = 1/6 J ≈ 0.1667 J, and the Parseval integral gives the same value, so the theorem is verified.
examples.check:
import math
E = 1.0/6.0
parseval = (1.0/(2.0*math.pi))*(math.pi/3.0)
print(E)
print(parseval)

traps: Missing the 1/2π in continuous-time Parseval. The transform pair convention decides the factor; with X(ω)=∫x(t)e^{−jωt}dt the factor is 1/2π.
Calling |X(ω)|² power for an energy signal. For finite-energy x(t), |X|² is an energy spectral density, not a power spectral density.
Mixing one-sided and two-sided axes. A two-sided integral over ω includes negative frequencies; a one-sided plot needs a factor 2 for the same band.
Using a continuous integral for a periodic signal. Periodic power is a sum over discrete lines |cₙ|², not an integral over all ω.
Forgetting units. Energy is in J, average power in W, ESD in J per rad/s, PSD in W per rad/s.

quiz.q: State Parseval's theorem for an energy signal with Fourier transform X(ω).
quiz.a: E=∫|x(t)|²dt=(1/2π)∫|X(ω)|²dω, where E is total energy in J and ω is in rad/s.

quiz.q: Why does continuous-time Parseval carry the factor 1/2π when ω is in rad/s?
quiz.a: The inverse Fourier transform has 1/2π in front. The frequency axis is in rad/s. If frequency f is in Hz, the factor disappears and E=∫|X(f)|²df.

quiz.q: For x(t)=e^{−2t}u(t), find the total energy E using X(ω)=1/(2+jω).
A periodic signal has c0=0, c1=0.5, c−1=0.5, and all other cₙ=0. Find its average power P.
An energy signal has ESD equal to K for |ω|≤B and zero outside. Express total energy E in terms of K and B.
Distinguish ESD from PSD in one sentence each.
quiz.a: ESD=|X(ω)|² applies to a finite-energy signal and has units J per rad/s. PSD=lim|X_T(ω)|²/T applies to a finite-power signal and has units W per rad/s.

quiz.q: A signal has E=10 J. A band |ω|≤B holds 90% of the energy. Write the integral condition for B.

beyond: Not for the exam. Practical spectrum analyzers estimate PSD with Welch's method: split the record, window each part, average periodograms. ECG and EEG analysis uses band power from PSD; machine vibration monitoring uses the same area-under-curve idea. Search 'Welch periodogram', 'energy spectral density', and 'Parseval theorem units'.
